mainText:
New Zealand's economy grew by zero point two percent in the June quarter, the lead story today.

New Zealand.

New Zealand's economy grew zero point two percent in the June quarter, RNZ reports. The country appears to have avoided major damage from the Middle East conflict and the fuel price shock that dominated the quarter. Canterbury has reclaimed top spot in the ASB Regional Economic Scoreboard, with Taranaki surging to second and Auckland falling to sixth. Wellington sits at the bottom of the rankings.

The government and Auckland's mayor want to scrap height limits for Auckland's central business district, to take advantage of the new City Rail Link. Proposals could add seventeen thousand homes and thirty seven thousand two hundred jobs to the city centre. Both RNZ and Stuff report the sweeping planning change.

Fire and Emergency's minister, Brooke van Velden, has questioned the agency's chief executive over withheld information, saying it breached its own law on levy collections. A report has separately criticised the organisation for giving wrong answers to an inquiry into the fire engine fleet, and for spending two hundred and seventy five thousand dollars on public relations and lawyers. The FENZ board meets soon to respond. The Privileges Committee chair has called an urgent meeting over a leaked FENZ report, with just three sitting days left in this parliamentary term.

The Waitangi Tribunal says the government's school curriculum rewrite is ideological and breached multiple treaty principles, aided by people hostile to Māori knowledge. Labour has announced it would pause the curriculum overhaul and NCEA changes if elected, and create an independent body to lead decisions on what is taught.

Five Karangahape Road venues, including the long running Family Bar, have lost their liquor licences after police intervention. Family Bar has served Auckland's rainbow communities for more than twenty years.

Western Bay of Plenty will hold a byelection after councillor Alan Kurtovich resigned. He says the trigger was the council's Māori wards decision, and stands by the decision despite the cost of the byelection.

World.

Palestinians continue moving back into northern Gaza on foot after Israel opened a crossing through the military zone bisecting the enclave, the Wall Street Journal reports. United Nations experts say there are reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed war crimes in strikes on Iran earlier this year, including one on a school in Minab, according to the BBC and Al Jazeera. The experts also accuse Iran's own authorities of crimes against humanity in a crackdown on protests.

Rwanda backed rebels remain inside Goma in eastern Congo after overrunning Congolese troops, the Wall Street Journal reports. United Nations officials estimate more than one million displaced people are trapped inside the city.

Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis have traded attacks, with five people killed, Al Jazeera reports. The Houthis say they struck Saudi Aramco facilities at Jizan and Yanbu. Saudi Arabia accuses the group of targeting Mecca, which the Houthis call a lie. Shipping companies remain wary of Red Sea routes despite a Houthi pledge to end targeting vessels, the Wall Street Journal reports.

Sweden's prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has resigned after an election loss. Left wing opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson look set to form the next government, the BBC reports.

Technology.

King Charles has warned artificial intelligence poses an existential danger if it falls into the wrong hands, speaking at a summit in Scotland with leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Nvidia. Microsoft AI head Mustafa Suleyman warned uncontrolled AI could lead to a rival silicon species. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the world is right to be afraid of the technology but should trust AI firms to manage it. Separately, OpenAI has disclosed six more safety issues and unveiled a new system to track, investigate and disclose cases of its models misbehaving.

Sport.

League. The Warriors beat Newcastle at Eden Park on Sunday in their sudden death elimination final. Sold out despite the switch to the bigger venue. They now advance in the NRL finals.

Rugby. The Black Ferns made mass changes for Sunday morning's WXV Global Series test against Scotland, with two potential debutants named. Result carries as a matter of record from the weekend fixture.

Golf. Ryan Fox has outgunned Rory McIlroy in the opening round of the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, in his first event in England since winning the Open Championship. Aaron Rai leads on six under sixty six, sharing top spot with Sweden's Joakim Lagergren. McIlroy stumbled late in his round.

Netball. Dame Noeline Taurua has been reappointed as Silver Ferns coach through to the twenty twenty seven World Cup. It follows a year after she was stood down amid a dispute with Netball New Zealand, and comes after she led the Ferns to gold in Glasgow.

Cycling. Top New Zealand rider Finn Fisher-Black has questioned Cycling New Zealand's policy of not funding athletes to attend the Road World Championships, warning it could push riders to prioritise their own ambitions over the national team.

Basketball. The Breakers have signed Mojave King as a replacement for injured American import Josiah-Jordan James, who will miss the start of the NBL season.

Coming up. NRL finals continue this week following the Warriors' win over Newcastle. The BMW PGA Championship continues at Wentworth. The Black Ferns' WXV Global Series campaign continues against Scotland.

End of flash.
